config.title: Container With Most Water

intro.title: Container With Most Water
intro.body: In this lesson, you will implement an algorithm to solve the 'Container With Most Water' lesson, which involves finding two lines on a 2D plane that can hold the maximum amount of water between them. You will learn the core concept of the two-pointer technique, an efficient approach for scanning arrays. The main constructs you'll use are arrays, loops, and conditional logic in JavaScript. By the end, you'll be able to write a function that calculates the maximum water area and understand how to optimize such solutions.
intro.usecase: The Container With Most Water algorithm is essential for optimizing space allocation in UI layouts and data visualization tools. For example, in dashboard design systems, this algorithm helps determine the maximum display area for charts or panels within constrained screen dimensions. It's also used in image cropping interfaces to find the largest rectangular area that maintains aspect ratios, and in responsive web components that need to dynamically calculate optimal container sizes. Understanding this pattern enables developers to build more efficient, space-aware interfaces that automatically adapt to different viewport constraints.

objectives: Initialize two pointers to represent the left and right boundaries of the container
Manipulate pointer positions to explore different container configurations
Apply the area calculation formula using height and width constraints
Construct a loop that iterates through possible container arrangements
Update the maximum area value when a larger container is found
Control pointer movement based on height comparisons to optimize the search
Implement the complete algorithm that returns the maximum water container area

content.body: Imagine you have a series of vertical lines of different heights. Your goal is to find the two lines that, together with the x-axis, form the container that can hold the most water. This is a classic two-pointer lesson where we'll move two positions through the data to find the optimal solution efficiently.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply the two-pointer technique to find maximum area between vertical lines
• Implement the pointer movement logic based on height comparisons
• Explain why moving the shorter pointer inward is optimal
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Look at these vertical lines: heights = [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]. Place two fingers on the first and last lines (positions 0 and 8). The width is 8, height is min(1, 7) = 1, so area = 8. Can you find a pair that gives more water?
content.title: Try it

content.body: Try moving your fingers inward. If you move the left finger to position 1 (height 8) and keep right at 8 (height 7), width = 7, height = min(8, 7) = 7, area = 49. That's much better! But is this the maximum? Keep exploring different pairs.
content.title: Explore possibilities

content.body: Notice something important: when you have two pointers, the area is limited by the shorter line. If you move the taller pointer inward, the width decreases but the height might stay the same or get smaller. What happens if you always move the shorter pointer instead?
content.title: Pattern recognition

content.body: You manually explored different pairs of lines, calculating areas by considering width and the minimum height. This is essentially checking all possible pairs - a brute force approach that would be O(n²) for n lines.
content.title: What you did

content.body: With 10,000 lines, checking every pair would mean about 50 million calculations. That's too slow! We need a smarter way that examines far fewer possibilities while still finding the maximum area.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Two positions moving through the data. We start with pointers at both ends and move them toward each other. The key insight: always move the shorter pointer inward because moving the taller one can only decrease the area (width decreases, height limited by shorter line).
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Two fingers on the array; move them according to the comparison of heights.

content.body: We'll use two pointers starting at the ends. Calculate area, update maximum. Then move the pointer pointing to the shorter line inward. Repeat until pointers meet. This single pass O(n) approach guarantees we find the maximum without checking all pairs.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Start with left = 0, right = last index, maxArea = 0
2. While left < right:
   a. Calculate width = right - left
   b. Calculate height = min(height[left], height[right])
   c. Calculate area = width × height
   d. Update maxArea if area is larger
   e. If height[left] < height[right], move left++
   f. Otherwise, move right--
3. Return maxArea

content.body: Great work! You've implemented the Container With Most Water solution using the two-pointer technique. Remember: always move the shorter pointer inward because the area is limited by the shorter height. This O(n) approach is much faster than checking all O(n²) pairs. The two-pointer pattern is powerful for many array lessons where you need to compare elements from different positions.
